text:
Unpopular opinion: most project managers are expensive note-takers.

They don't build. They don't sell. They schedule the people who do, then take the credit in the QBR.

I've worked with 40+ of them. Three were worth the salary.

Tell me I'm wrong.

Remote work is dead.

The people still defending it are the ones who were never that productive in an office either. Your calendar is empty, your camera is off, and your output is a Slack emoji.

Come back or get replaced. Those are the options.

If you need a 4-day week to do good work, the calendar isn't your problem.

You are.

Every high performer I know works more than they admit and enjoys it. The rest invented a movement so they could feel virtuous about doing less.

Half of the "AI experts" on this platform learned everything they know from a 20-minute YouTube video last Tuesday.

You can tell, because they all say the same three things about agents, and none of them has ever shipped one to a paying customer.

Comment "builder" if you actually have.

Your company doesn't have a hiring problem.

It has a "nobody wants to work for you" problem.

7 interview rounds. A take-home that takes a weekend. "Competitive salary" with no number. And then you post about the talent shortage. 🤡

Bootcamps are a scam.

There, I said it. €12k for a Udemy playlist and a Discord server, sold to people who can't afford to lose €12k.

Go ahead, bootcamp founders, tell me about your 94% placement rate again.

If you're still telling 18-year-olds to spend four years and €40,000 on a computer science degree, you are stealing from them.

The degree taught you discipline? No. It taught you debt.

Every recruiter who ghosts a candidate after a third interview should be barred from the profession.

Not "should apologise". Barred.

You had time for four calls and no time for one email. We see you.

Founders who post about their 5am routines have never run anything harder than a Notion board.

Cold plunge, journaling, 400 push-ups, and a company doing €0 in revenue.

Wake up at 9 and ship something.

Agile is a cult.

Standups, retros, story points, velocity charts — a whole priesthood built to make managers feel involved in work they don't understand.

Change my mind. I'll wait in the comments.

A meeting that could have been an email doesn't mean your manager is busy.

It means your manager is useless.

If your only contribution to the product is a recurring calendar invite, you are overhead with a job title.

The "quiet quitting" crowd would have been fired in 2005. And rightly so.

Doing the bare minimum used to be called doing the bare minimum. Now it has a hashtag and a LinkedIn fan club.

Nobody in this industry is burned out.

They're bored, badly managed, and addicted to their phones.

Fight me.

Tell me you've never shipped anything without telling me you've never shipped anything:

put "Strategic Visionary | Thought Leader | Disruptor" in your headline.

Every single time. Every. Single. Time.

Your SaaS product is not disrupting anything.

It's a spreadsheet with a login page and a €49/month subscription.

I said what I said.

Junior developers today cannot code without an AI.

In five years there won't be a single engineer under 30 who can debug a null pointer without asking a chatbot for permission.

The seniors who let this happen will be the ones cleaning it up.

Open-plan offices were designed by people who don't work in them, and are defended by people who enjoy watching you.

If you brought yours back, you didn't make a real estate decision. You made a trust announcement.

Most "thought leaders" on here would not survive one sprint on a real team.

No ticket. No on-call. No angry customer. Just a carousel post about resilience.

Prove me wrong.

Unlimited PTO is a scam.

It isn't generosity, it's an accounting trick so the company never has to pay out your unused days when you leave.

Ask your HR director to confirm it in writing. Watch what happens.

Stop calling yourself an engineer if you can't explain what happens when you type a URL into a browser.

Harsh? Maybe. True? Also yes.

We measured our hiring funnel this quarter and the numbers surprised us.

812 applications, 37 first screens, 11 technical rounds, 4 offers, 2 accepted.

The drop-off wasn't where we expected: it was between the screen and the technical round, where candidates waited an average of 9 days. We've cut that to 48 hours and will report back in March.

I disagree with the timeline in the AI Act implementing acts, specifically Article 6(3) and the classification carve-out.

In practice, a provider can self-declare a system out of scope before any documentation exists, and the notified body only sees it afterwards. That order is backwards, and the December date makes it worse.

Written comments are open until the 14th; ours are linked below.

Today we let go of 34 colleagues, about 12% of the company.

We over-hired in 2024 against a revenue plan we did not hit. That was my decision and my mistake, not theirs.

Everyone affected has 3 months' salary, keeps their laptop, and has an open reference from me. A list of people looking for work is in the comments; they are excellent.

Your CV is too long.

Two pages, numbers first, no photo, no skills bar charts. A recruiter gives it about 20 seconds.

"Reduced reconciliation from 3 hours to 11 minutes" beats "detail-oriented team player" every time.

Another week, another headline saying AI will replace developers.

So we measured it. Six months, 41 engineers, Copilot and Cursor enabled for everyone.

PRs per engineer up 18%. Review time per PR up 26%. Net throughput roughly flat, with more time spent reading code than writing it. Useful, not revolutionary. Full write-up with the methodology in the link.

After 11 years I've changed my mind about unit tests.

On our billing module, 214 unit tests missed a provincial tax rule that ran wrong in production for 11 months. Three integration tests would have caught it.

I still write unit tests for pure functions. I no longer treat coverage as a quality metric.

We're releasing Ocean, our image-processing library, under an MIT licence today.

It was built for mobile: small binary, ARM-optimised, with sample apps for iOS and Android. Docs and benchmarks are in the repo.

Issues and PRs welcome, and the team will be answering them this week.

I bought a used car last month and had it inspected first. The mechanic found uneven tyre wear and a CV boot starting to tear, and the seller dropped the price by €900.

The inspection cost €150. I mention it because I nearly skipped it to close the deal that weekend.

A note on the benchmark in Table 3 of the paper: the baseline was trained for 40k steps and the proposed model for 120k, on the same budget graph.

When I matched the step count, the gap fell from 4.1 to 0.6 BLEU. Code to reproduce is in the thread; I'd welcome a correction if I've misread the setup.

Our Scope 1 and 2 emissions fell 19% last year, and Scope 3 rose 4%.

The rise is freight, mostly air freight we added to hit delivery promises in Q4. We are not going to pretend that nets out to progress. The full report, including the numbers we'd rather not publish, is linked.

We're hiring a senior data engineer in Lyon, hybrid, €65-78k depending on experience.

Python, dbt, Snowflake. You'd own the ingestion pipelines end to end, on a team of five. Two interviews, no take-home.

Apply through the link; I read every application.

I was wrong about Kubernetes.

I argued for two years that our four services didn't need it, and I was right about the complexity and wrong about the direction: we now run 30 services and the migration we postponed cost us six weeks of downtime risk.

If your service count is growing 3x a year, start earlier than feels reasonable.

Back from PyCon with three pages of notes.

The talk on typed dataframes changed how I'll structure our ETL, and the hallway conversation about flaky test triage was worth the flight on its own. Slides from my session are linked, including the parts that didn't work.

We raised prices 20% in March and expected churn to spike. It didn't.

Monthly churn went from 2.4% to 2.5%, inside the noise. Expansion revenue rose, because the customers who stayed moved to annual.

The cohort data is in the post, including the two segments where churn did rise.

Honest review of the tool we trialled for six weeks, since I was asked in DMs.

Import worked well, the API is clean and the support team answered within a day. Reporting is weak: no custom date ranges, and exports cap at 10k rows, which broke our month-end.

We're not renewing, but I'd recommend it to a smaller team.

Our flight was cancelled at 23:40 and the airline rebooked 180 passengers onto a plane with 60 seats.

I've filed under EU261 with the booking reference and the delay confirmation. Posting the process here because three colleagues asked, not to start a pile-on: the form takes ten minutes and the payment arrived in seven weeks.

Maya joined us from a bootcamp in 2022 and asked, on day one, why we stored tokens the way we did.

That question turned into a security review and a move to standards-based OAuth2. She's now leading the auth work.

If you're mentoring someone this year: the question they're embarrassed to ask is usually the useful one.

Last week we finish the migration of our old system to the new one. Is not perfect but it works and the team do a great job during three months.

Thank you to everybody who help, specially the support team who answer all the tickets in this period. Next step is the reporting module in January.

This month's newsletter is out: the AI Act timeline, two papers on retrieval evaluation, and a short piece on why our latency budget moved.

About 1,200 words, once a month, no sponsorships. Link in the first comment.

Geothermal is the most underrated part of the energy transition, and I think the cost curve is about to bend.

The drilling techniques from shale transfer directly, the resource is everywhere, and the permitting fight is smaller than for wind. The counter-argument, which I take seriously, is that nobody has yet shown it at scale outside Iceland. Article linked.
